question: This is Zach Ogden on for Andrew. So Adam, last quarter you brought up the idea of changing the pricing strategy from one per year to more of a learn and go approach. So one, is that the strategy for 2026? And then two, is this a change in philosophy that you are prioritizing traffic growth over margin expansion? Or is, let's say, the high twenties restaurant margin at $4 million AUV still feasible and, I guess, assuming normalized inflation?
answer: So as you know, we are currently running price of about 2% from the increase that we took in December. And that has been enough to really offset the underlying inflation we have seen so far this year. And that compares to the 4% that the industry is running as a whole. So it is really great how we have been able to offset underlying inflation while also increasing our value gap. And something that we have done historically, and we want to continue to do in the future. But as we look into next year, as we mentioned in our prepared comments, inflation is stepping up into that mid-single-digit range. So, given the elevated inflation and the ongoing consumer uncertainty, we are going to take a slow and measured approach to pricing in 2026. And I think that is kind of what you are getting at is we are going to kind of take it over time rather than all at once. And at this point, we do not plan to fully offset inflation in 2026. And so this will pressure margins in the near term, but we believe it is the right thing to do for our guests in this environment. It will further increase our value proposition and will create a temporary dislocation, but we believe that we can get that back over time. I believe, Zach, you also had a question, a follow-up question about our long-term algorithm that we have talked about quite extensively. It will always be our endeavor, regardless of what is going on with the economy, to expand our margins responsibly based on the flow through historically …
asks: [answered*] Whether the 2026 pricing strategy is to move from one annual increase to a slower, learn-and-go approach | [partial] Whether management is prioritizing traffic growth over margin expansion, and whether high-twenties restaurant margins at $4 million AUV remain feasible under normalized inflation
rationale: They clearly answered the 2026 pricing approach, but only gave a general long-term margin framework, not a direct answer on traffic-vs-margin priority or the specific high-twenties margin feasibility.
my_note: Confirmed a slow, measured 2026 pricing rollout that won't fully offset inflation, but gave a generic long-term margin spiel instead of addressing whether high-twenties margins at $4M AUV remain feasible.

question: And then, Scott, the last couple of calls, you have expressed confidence in returning to mid-single-digit same-store sales. So is that still the case for 2026? Or, I guess, what would be a reasonable time to get back there?
answer: I believe that it is. It will all depend on what is going on in the consumer backdrop. Likely to be the toughest for the consumers. The economists we have spoken to over the last several quarters say Q4, Q1, specifically, the cohort under $100,000 annually, which I talked about in prepared remarks. And then some easing in Q2. So I do not have a crystal ball, but here is what I will tell you. Our aim is to continue to be a transaction-led growth company. Full stop. And we are confident in our ability to get back there through the acceleration of the consumer flywheel I talk about often: operations, digital, and marketing.
asks: [answered*] Whether returning to mid-single-digit same-store sales is still the plan for 2026 | [partial] What would be a reasonable time to get back to mid-single-digit same-store sales
rationale: He reaffirmed the goal, but only gave broad macro timing commentary, not a clear timeframe for reaching mid-single-digit same-store sales.
my_note: Reaffirmed confidence in returning to mid-single-digit comps via the consumer flywheel, but gave no concrete timeline beyond citing economist expectations of consumer easing in Q2.

question: If I could just start on the comp, I guess it is a fairly wide range of outcomes for Q4 with the down low single digit for the year. Can you just help level set where you exited the quarter and what you are seeing from a traffic perspective?
answer: I will start off on this one. So towards the July and into August, we experienced a step down like we talked about in our prepared comments. And that was somewhere around the two to 300 basis point range. And then as Scott mentioned in his prepared comments, we increased spend on our media as well as our promotions that helped offset some of the softness that we were seeing specifically in August and September. And we also saw a strong reaction when we launched carne asada and even red chimichurri in early October. However, during this whole time, the underlying transaction trend remained under pressure. And in recent weeks, it softened even further. So when you account for this recent trend as well as the ongoing uncertainty in the economy, the way that we are kind of looking at Q4 is really with a much more conservative view. And right now, at this point, we expect comps in Q4 to decline somewhere in the low to mid-single-digit range.
asks: [answered*] Level set Q4 comp outlook and where you exited the quarter | [answered] What traffic trends you’re seeing
rationale: Management gave the Q4 comp range and described recent traffic/transaction trends, including the step-down and further softness.
my_note: Laid out the July/August 200-300 bps step-down, recent transaction softening, and the resulting conservative Q4 comp expectation of down low- to mid-single digits.

question: When you look at what is going on with traffic, where are the losses really coming from? I understand some of the cohort commentary, but do you think you are also losing customers that are trading down or out of the space? Losing frequency of transactions with your more loyal customers?
answer: Lauren, I will tell you, based on the data that we have, we are seeing that significant pullback from that cohort under $100,000 annually. And, also, that age group 25 to 34, which we over-index to is about 25% of our total sales, has pulled back meaningfully. Based on our data, both purchased and in-house data, it shows that we are gaining market share, but that cohort, so meaning, we are not losing them to the competition. We are losing them to grocery and food at home. And so that consumer is under pressure. It is one of our core consumer cohorts. And so they feel the pinch, and we feel the pullback from them as well. We were able to reengage them through the Summer of Extras promotion that we ran both through our loyalty rewards campaign as well as some digital initiatives that we did around Chipotle IQ as well as FreePotle. So we know with the right activations, we can get that consumer back into our business. And we are going to leverage what we have learned from Summer of Extras to really inform the 2026 digital strategy.
asks: [answered*] Where traffic losses are really coming from | [partial] Whether customers are trading down/out of the space or loyal customers are buying less often
rationale: Management identified the weak cohorts and said the loss is to grocery/food at home, but only partly addressed trading-down and loyal-frequency dynamics.
my_note: Used internal and purchased data to show they are gaining restaurant share and losing frequency specifically among <$100k and 25-34 cohorts to grocery/food at home rather than competitors.

question: Thanks for taking the question. I wanted to delve into the kind of HEAT throughput that you are seeing at the pilot locations. Can you talk about how meaningful that has been? I think you referred to it potentially yielding a step function in throughput, and I am curious as to what the actual results are.
answer: So we are still early innings, unfortunately. We are in 75 restaurants today, another 100 this quarter. And then we will start with all new restaurant openings, as I said on the previous call. Here going forward. And so it gives us a lot of optimism around the project as we are already seeing labor efficiency gains. We are seeing better culinary, better food scores, better guest experience scores. We are seeing better delivery of distribution of labor during peak hours, which is leading to improved throughput for those restaurants. I cannot get into specifics at present, but all signs are pointing up into the right.

question: And a follow-up on the price question. Is it fair to assume that you are going to exit the year with no price at this point?
answer: Let us say, at this point, we are going to look maybe later in the quarter at starting to understand some of the impacts of price. So you might see us test in a small number of restaurants. But expect the two points of price that we are running right now to fall off in December. That is kind of how we are looking at it towards the end of the year. But it is still kind of fluid at this point.
asks: [partial*] Whether it's fair to assume the company will exit the year with no price in place | [answered] Any planned price tests later in the quarter

question: Scott, since the consumer environment is deteriorating and the menu marketing efforts are not fully offsetting the traffic retraction, while the LTOs, dips, and marketing uplift may be helping traffic in '26, can you help us understand and maybe expand on the operational actions that you are taking in the near term to be inflecting the traffic regardless of the macro action?
answer: So thank you for the question, Bill. I will tell you we ran a problem detection study. We actually renewed our problem detection study over the last quarter, which highlighted some key operational concerns that we are addressing as we speak. Jason Kidd, as you know, is probably just over a hundred and twenty days in as Chief Operating Officer. And I will tell you, he is quickly gathered the team, rallied the teams. They truly respect his leadership and his approach. And the problems that we have identified, he and the teams are actively working against solutions for those problems, as well as modifying our quarterly bonus program incentives target specifically for our restaurant teams to tie to the outcomes that we want to see going forward. So it is all grounded in this new strategy that I referenced very quickly at the end of the call around Recipe for Growth. And it is a three-pronged strategy. Of course, it includes operations, digital, and marketing. So from an operations perspective, we are digging in on what are the main friction points for the consumer today because they are different than they were just a year ago. It is my belief that the consumer that is in the market today is more discerning. They are looking for value and not necessarily value as a price point, but value as a benefit over price. I talk about that a lot. And so we have to over-deliver on those expectations in this consumer environment. And I promise you, my operations team under Jason's leadership …
asks: [partial*] What near-term operational actions are being taken to inflect traffic despite the macro
rationale: Management outlined several initiatives, but mostly at a high level. It did not give a detailed near-term operational playbook for traffic inflection independent of macro.
my_note: Mentioned a problem detection study, new COO leadership, and tweaking store bonus incentives, but stayed at a high strategic level rather than detailing specific operational fixes.

question: Also add, you know, one extra spin on that or rev on that is we are rapidly increasing the pace of innovation as it relates to culinary innovation. And so you will see more in 2026 because we know new news is really resonating with core consumers today. Excellent. Thank you, Scott. And maybe, Adam, I was wondering if you can update us on the ROIC of incremental units being built. Specifically, if today you are seeing more cannibalization on your existing stores versus the past, and if the 8 to 10% net unit growth guidance that you shared for the long term is still reasonable today or if there is any capacity constraint or return constraint that will make you think that the 8 to 10% may not be achievable going forward.
answer: So, no, in terms of, you know, impact that new restaurants are having on our existing restaurants, on a per restaurant basis or a per new restaurant basis, we are seeing very similar levels to what we have in the past. The overall impact as it impacts our overall comp is increasing as we increase that percentage growth over time. But that is natural as you kind of go up in that. And then plus those new restaurants drive a much higher comp. They comp much better than our existing restaurants, so that helps offset that. So net-net, you are seeing about a 100 basis point or so impact to our overall comps from this NRL growth. And then, Scott, do you want to talk about in terms of kind of the pace that we are at? I think that was the part. And I will tell you that 1% has been historical for the last ten or fifteen years is what we typically see in a given year regardless of the number of openings. But I will tell you, you know, it is a great question. You know, we believe we have reached the right pace that enables us to consistently open the best locations, staff with the most talented teams, to maintain industry-leading unit economics and returns. And I do not know of anyone else in the space that is growing at that clip. If you frame it in this reference point, it is a rough every twenty-four hours, which is incredible growth. And we feel really comfortable in that as a sweet spot. And it does not mean we will not flex up, Danilo, but we feel great in that range today.
asks: [answered*] Update on ROIC of incremental new units, including whether new restaurants are cannibalizing existing stores more than before | [answered] Whether the long-term 8% to 10% net unit growth guidance is still reasonable | [answered] Whether there are any capacity or return constraints that would make 8% to 10% unachievable
rationale: Management said cannibalization is similar to history, quantified the comp drag, and affirmed the growth range remains workable with current capacity and returns.
my_note: Quantified cannibalization at the historical ~100 bps comp drag and confirmed unit economics, staffing, and returns comfortably support 8%-10% unit growth.

question: I am trying to put this into a question. In the near term, it obviously, you are sacrificing incremental margins. You know, some of this is comps. You know, you are pointing to low to mid-single-digit same-store sales declines in the quarter. And some of it is some outsized inflation. But some of it is also that, you know, you are trying to not price to that inflation and perhaps give better or work towards a better value for the consumer. And hopefully, over time, maybe get recognized for that. And wondering what that could mean for '20. You mentioned that incremental margins would be you are still thinking 40% long term, but it also feels like in the near term, that is not going to be the case, that you are maybe going to earn the right to get back to that incremental margin by maybe rebasing those restaurant margins into 2026 as we find perhaps some stability in traffic and your core consumer can find their own footing in terms of their own economic well-being. I am just wondering how we should be thinking about that, where we might sort of find a base in terms of restaurant margin, and just broadly speaking, how you are thinking about this because, you know, or is this do you think that the solution really is going to be just giving better value to the consumer? You know, you have tried all these other levers. This is based going to be about just giving better food value and then eventually, you are just going to start to really comp strongly again because the is a very good brand. Wonder how you are thinking about all that.
answer: You are heading down the right path. You know, I will tell you the core value proposition that is Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. is still firmly intact. And the business fundamentals are still strong. And, you know, what we are faced with today, we talk a lot about this, is while we have opportunities, we believe that the consumer slowdown is really affecting our business in a meaningful way. But we would never let a good crisis go to waste, David. I think you and I have talked about in the past. We are going to double down our efforts on the consumer flywheel, ensure we are delivering on value in the most meaningful way in this environment, and we will emerge stronger as an organization than we were when we went into this consumer slowdown. And so if we need to invest some component of margin to really drive top-line transactions in the near term, David, there could be something there. Again, you know, not being able to price against the inflation that we will see next year is one leg of that. And so once we believe that the consumer is on better footing, we will do what is right and appropriate for the business and for the consumer to get back to our long-term algo. Anything you would add to that, Adam? I mean, just a reminder that as you know, David, I mean, we take price to offset the impact of inflation, and then we are going to drive that margin north with transaction growth. I mean, this has been our approach in the past. It will continue to be our approach in the future …
asks: [partial*] How to think about near-term incremental margins and where restaurant margins may base out, including what that implies for 2026 | [answered] Whether the main solution is simply delivering better value to consumers | [answered] Whether incremental margins can ultimately return to the long-term 40% flow-through as comps and transactions recover
rationale: Management explained the value strategy and reiterated long-term 40% flow-through, but did not give a specific near-term margin base or 2026 target.
my_note: Validated the strategy of investing margin in value and reiterated long-term 40% flow-through, but avoided giving a restaurant margin floor or 2026 target.

question: Thanks for taking the question. I wanted to ask another one on 2026, maybe asking it in a different way. But Adam or Scott, any guardrails on how you are thinking about 2026 from a comps perspective or maybe traffic and the timeline getting back to positive traffic or maybe how you are thinking about the shape of the year when considering the comparisons, pricing dynamics, and all the internal initiatives for next year. But one thing that I would say that is important to note is, as you know, we have had several underlying step downs throughout the year. So you have got to take this into account, and if you do that, you will come up with a baseline in 2026 that starts negative. But then we are confident that we can build upon that with the initiatives that we have in place for 2026. Get that north of there. And, Scott, if you want to comment on some of those. Here is what I would tell you. In the Recipe for Growth strategy, just think about it as we are developing a road map of initiatives with clear ownership expectations and deliverables that will serve as our top enterprise priorities for the year. The good news is it aligns with our five strategic priorities, and we will use it to accelerate the consumer flywheel that you hear me talk about often, which will strengthen our value proposition and really get us back to mid-sing …

my_note: Explained why 2026 starts with a negative comp baseline due to 2025 step-downs, but deferred formal guidance to February and gave no timeline for turning traffic positive.

question: I have, I guess, a two-part question. The first is just about the value proposition. And, Scott, you said, you know, the fast-casual is being viewed as perhaps not as unaffordable. But I guess trying to reconcile that with the idea that you are not really losing share of restaurant wallet to either QSRs or casual diners or your peers. It actually sounds like maybe the value proposition is appreciated. And so I was just curious where you are kind of seeing that feedback about fast-casual because it is not showing up in your share. And I guess on that same note, do you see any difference in daypart? Like, lunch versus dinner? You know, we have heard now that weekday lunch is perhaps weaker just because of, you know, it is easier to give up. So anything there?
answer: Thanks for the question. You know, dayparts are holding up very consistently, roughly fifty-fifty between lunch and dinner. So no meaningful shift there. I will tell you candidly through our problem detection study, there were a few remarks that said that the brand was unaffordable. And I think they were broad-based in general, but I am curious to know, you know, further, does that consumer believe us to be lumped in with other, you know, casual or fast-casual concepts at the $15 price point, which just is not true. And so while I am not going to disparage the or have a price-pointed ad, I do want to communicate that you can get extraordinary value for around $10 at Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. in a way that does not say what I just said. And that is the challenge.

rationale: Gave a direct daypart read and noted some affordability comments, but did not fully explain the source or reconcile the value-proposition/share question.
my_note: Directly answered the daypart question (holding steady at 50/50 lunch/dinner), but only speculated on why survey respondents lumped Chipotle in with $15 fast-casual peers despite stable share.

question: So just to follow-up on that, as you talk about, you know, things that you have trialed in terms of how do you communicate value, can you give me any sense like is it you are doing through social media or targeted marketing through your app? Just, you know, the idea of communicating value without a price point, it seems a little bit tricky to me.
answer: You know, we did test that ad I just mentioned to you. Where we showed a lot of abundance. We showed classic culinary. And we showed consumers eating Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. And we said at the end of the ad, you can get all this for around $10. And in the testing, the consumer missed that message point altogether. And said that is really not meaningful to me. What was meaningful to me was looking at innovation, looking at culinary, and looking at what makes Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. special and unique. I think there is more work to do, and Chris will tell you he has got, you know, several work streams underway to really ferret out what is the right approach. We are engaging other ad agencies to bring in ideas to ensure we have the best thinking in the room. But we will you will see some new ads and a new strategy in 2026.

question: Scott, I wanted to come back to some of the comments around menu innovation looking to 2026 for what sounds like at least one, maybe two incremental LTOs that I think you had mentioned. Any other learnings maybe from the '25 LTO launches to help you think about those launches next year in the current environment to maximize impact, whether it is something with marketing or timing or anything like that? Obviously, you guys have a long track record under your leadership of successfully launching LTOs. You have done it well historically. Just anything new given the environment that in takeaways from this year as you think about ramping up those launches next year?
answer: It is a great question. You know, here is what I will tell you. Is the repeat LTOs still performed well. Well, the initial transaction lift seemed to be muted because of the consumer backdrop. Each one did drive transaction and spend in incidents. And we also learned this year that a consumer that buys an LTOs lifetime value goes up exponentially. Meaning, they are going to spend more throughout the year than a consumer that does not purchase an LTO. What gives me a lot of confidence in the 2026 strategy of what surprised me this year was the success around dips. And so Adobo Ranch was highly successful. Red chimichurri is proving to be just as, if not more successful. It is even driving an incremental trial on carne asada. What is exciting about 2026 is there could be a blend of new innovation as well as historic innovation that has worked really, really well. But at the end of the day, what we know is working is new news and new product news and product innovation. So we are going to lean into that more meaningfully in the coming year. So you will see not only LTOs around proteins, but you will also see us pepper in sauces, dips, or sides that we think will have a step change improvement in the consumer experience.
asks: [answered*] Learnings from 2025 LTO launches to improve 2026 launches in the current environment, including marketing/timing implications
rationale: He gave concrete learnings from 2025 and explained how they shape 2026 innovation and LTO mix; no explicit marketing/timing detail, but the core ask was addressed.
my_note: Detailed key takeaways (LTO buyers have higher annual LTV; dips like Adobo Ranch and Red Chimichurri drove strong trial) and explained how 2026 will blend proteins with dips/sides.

question: Thanks for taking the question. Scott, you mentioned the locations with the new equipment are seeing improved guest satisfaction scores. But have you observed any concerning trends in customer set metrics for the rest of the chain, particularly regarding speed of service or food quality?
answer: Nothing that stands out as divergent. Here is what I will tell you is we are struggling in digital with accuracy. And I will tell you why. And I will tell you why I think that is. I think we made a shift in our annual incentive plan to focus on-time versus accuracy. Because we were doing pretty well in accuracy at the time we decided to make that change. Our accuracy has fallen off. And so we are redesigning the incentive plan to accurately target the right things that the if you think about if you think about the consumer needs states in digital specifically, it is give me what I ordered accurately on time. And high quality and in abundance. And it is very simple to deliver on those three need states, but you have to incentivize the right behavior for our 130,000 people in the field. And so we are shifting that back to accuracy. And as you can imagine, accuracy versus on-time is far more important. If you are five minutes late, but everything is in the bag, it is not that big of a deal. If you show up ten minutes early and my kids' quesadilla is missing, now we have a real problem. And so I do not think we are actively incentivizing the right behaviors, and so we are going to get back to what we know to be true about those consumer needs states.
asks: [partial*] Any concerning trends in customer set metrics across the rest of the chain, especially speed of service or food quality
rationale: He said there were no divergent trends, but only gave a related digital accuracy issue and not a direct read on speed of service or food quality.
my_note: Stated nothing stood out broadly on speed or food quality, then pivoted to a digital order-accuracy issue caused by incentive metrics without giving a direct read on speed or quality.

question: I understand the reluctance to price right now and to even talk about pricing in this environment, but I think we are trying to better understand what the action plan for pricing is when that 2% rolls off December into '26. I mean, you talk to us about how to think about the right base case or even the possible scenarios that you are thinking about for 2026 pricing against that mid-single-digit cost inflation?
answer: So I can jump in here. So as we talked about earlier, we want to take a slow and measured approach, and so what that ultimately means is, typically, in the past, you would see us take price across the country in one fell swoop maybe over a week or two. We are going to look at this over time. You know, it could be over four or five or six months. It could be over twelve months. It really depends on as we start to roll a certain amount of restaurants and get some good reads on what we understand the resistance to be, the reaction to be, we will determine from there. So that is why we are being a little bit vague because the strategy is still very fluid. But we do know it is not going to be what we have done in the past, which is all at once. And then that is kind of the general strategy in terms of the rollout. And then in terms of this mid-single-digit inflation that we alluded to, which is driven mostly by cost of sales, that number is much higher than what we have seen in the past. I mean, typically, we have seen a low single-digit inflation of around 2%, so that is giving us some caution with the consumer environment to not go that high too often like we typically have in the past, so we will be more patient with that over time. But we will continue to talk about this each quarter and give you updates as to kind of what we are at, what we are seeing, and what we are running. I do not think we have talked about nor are prepared to talk about risk mitigation strategies as it …
asks: [answered*] 2026 pricing action plan and rollout timing when the 2% rolls off | [partial] Base case or scenarios for pricing versus mid-single-digit cost inflation | [declined] Risk mitigation strategies to offset inflation
rationale: Management gave a clear pricing rollout approach and timing range, but only general color on inflation scenarios and explicitly declined detailed mitigation tactics.
my_note: Explained the staggered 4-to-12-month rollout mechanics, but declined to provide pricing scenarios against inflation or discuss inflation risk-mitigation tactics.

question: And as it relates to the unit growth, you are accelerating openings in '26 to a very impressive unprecedented level, clearly strong growth. Is there and I know you have talked a lot about historically the cannibalization factor and it has remained very, very steady. But does this at all elevate your risk and your ability to drive same-store traffic growth moving forward? Just given the multiple years of such high growth and the fact that is accelerating, what gives you confidence that you can execute on a same-store basis while opening this many units?
answer: So I can jump in here. So we definitely have the confidence we can still drive same-store sales, you know, even if that starts to, you know, that growth starts to basically level off at some point in the future as we approach 7,000 restaurants. Because you have to keep in mind, new restaurants do impact overall comp by that rough 100 basis points or so. So that is actually going to come down over time, and then our existing restaurants do a fantastic job of comping. We even see our restaurants that are over fifteen or twenty years comping as well when we are driving overall transactions up. So I do not think it is going to have any impact, if anything. It will start to give us a very small tailwind as that starts to level off. I would add to that. Yeah. One of the unique things about the Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. brand, having worked in other brands, the cannibalized restaurants at Chipotle Mexican Grill, Inc. recover inside of twelve to thirteen months.
